title: Starting over
hook: Zen: start again at one. Shenxiu's verse and Huineng's on the monastery wall, and the breath count that returns to one
tomorrow: a man crossed a flood on a raft. what did he do with it after?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: just start again. The father ran before the speech was done. Today, what starting again actually looks like, one breath at a time.
screen: `JUST START AGAIN.` → `ONE BREATH AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Someone writes a big idea on the office whiteboard overnight, and by morning everyone's talking about it. A Zen story starts like that. The Fifth Patriarch of Chan, the Chinese school that became Zen, tells his monks: write a verse that shows your understanding, and the one who truly sees will receive the robe. The head monk, Shenxiu, writes his at night on a corridor wall. Then a lay worker who pounds rice out back, and can't read, hears it, and asks someone to write a second verse beside it.
screen: `A BIG IDEA ON THE WHITEBOARD.` → `WRITE A VERSE, WIN THE ROBE.` → `SHENXIU WRITES AT NIGHT.` → `A RICE POUNDER ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Shenxiu's verse, in plain words: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it with care at all times, and let no dust gather. The rice pounder, Huineng, answered: awakening has no tree, the mirror has no stand; from the beginning there is not one thing, so where would dust gather? The Platform Sutra says the Patriarch gave Huineng the robe, secretly, by night. But that book comes from Huineng's heirs, and Shenxiu had students of his own. So let both speak. Shenxiu: dust really does gather. Wiping every day is honest about how a mind works. Huineng: there's nothing to get back to. The mind was never dirty, so every moment starts whole. Here's where they meet. One common Zen practice is counting breaths, one to ten. When you lose count, you go back to one. For Shenxiu, going back to one is the daily wiping. For Huineng, one isn't a step backward, because nothing was lost. Either way the Zen instruction is the same: no scolding, no catching up. Start again at one.
screen: `WIPE THE MIRROR AT ALL TIMES.` · `FROM THE BEGINNING, NOT ONE THING.` · `SHENXIU: DUST REALLY GATHERS.` · `HUINENG: NOTHING WAS LOST.` · then, large: `AT ONE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if you like, and count your out-breaths, one to ten. When you reach ten, or lose the count, go back to one, without a word to yourself about it. Keep counting until the bell.
Starting over: going back to one, as in Zen breath counting, whether you hear it as wiping the mirror or as nothing lost.
Your line: at one. Lose the count, begin again, no catching up. Day 1676, from one.

howItsDone: A common Zen sitting instruction is to count breaths from one to ten and return to one whenever you lose count. The verses of Shenxiu and Huineng come from the Platform Sutra.

fork.setup: a friend in your meditation group says: my mind is a mess, so I have to wipe the mirror every single day. what's the best case for Huineng's side?
options: nothing was ever lost, so each start is whole; no need to make up for a messy day.
daily practice is pointless, so you might as well stop.
dust isn't real, so mistakes don't matter at all.
fork.reveal: Huineng's verse says there is not one thing for dust to land on. Shenxiu says wipe every day. Both send you back to one.

trapdoor: what you thought: starting over means losing all your progress.
what it means: in Zen breath counting you go back to one, either as daily wiping (Shenxiu) or because nothing was lost (Huineng).
what a scholar hears: the Platform Sutra, a text of Huineng's Southern school; Shenxiu led the Northern school, later cast as 'gradual.'

chat.says: restarted my sit. lost count at like 4, six times. i'm worse than when i started
options: go back to one each time. in Zen, returning to one is the practice, not the failure.

chat.meaning: Zen breath counting returns to one whenever you lose count. Shenxiu would call it wiping the mirror; Huineng, proof that nothing was lost.

tie.story: Shenxiu said wipe the mirror at all times; Huineng said there's not one thing to dust. Both views send you back to one.
tie.friend: Zoe losing count six times is six returns to one, not proof she's getting worse.
tie.you: where could you start again at one today?

Fifth Patriarch.meaning: the fifth teacher in Chan's line, who set the verse test

Chan.meaning: the Chinese school of Buddhism that became Zen in Japan

Shenxiu.meaning: the head monk who wrote the first verse

Huineng.meaning: the rice pounder whose verse won the robe

Platform Sutra.meaning: the Chan text that tells Huineng's story and teaching
